body.text: The talk at Alastair Campbell’s National Press Club address this week in Canberra quickly got around to sandpapergate. The scandal itself, now eight years old, hardly needs summarising, but the recent publication of former cricketer Usman Khawaja’s autobiography — with its claim that the whole Australian side knew sandpaper was being used to cheat during the 2018 South African tour — has propelled the story back into global headlines.

Making light of the saga, Campbell began his address by wryly brandishing a square of sandpaper. The affair was, he later remarked, a classic case of “man writes book” and then “newspapers find book very interesting.” Without likening it to the debates about Australian SAS war crimes in Afghanistan (as others have done recently), he identified in the controversy core human themes such as “truth” and “lying,” “accountability” and the “breakdown of teamship.”

Twenty years ago, it would have been hard to predict that Alastair Campbell — the British journalist who became Tony Blair’s high-profile Downing Street communications director — would be a global political celebrity in his own right. That he would be sought after for comment on the Australian cricket team’s integrity would have seemed even less likely. (But then again, who could have predicted that America’s then-president George W. Bush would now seem like a worldly intellectual in comparison with recent incumbents?)

Campbell’s reach has grown exponentially. In the late 2000s, his abridged account of the Blair years sold around 230,000 copies; British hoteliers reported it as the title most frequently abandoned in hotel rooms by departing guests. (Khawaja’s Sabr seems less likely to face that problem.) By the mid 2010s, Campbell was writing for men’s magazine GQ’s monthly audience of more than 117,000 and had a YouTube following of several hundred thousand.

Launched in 2022, the podcast he co-hosts, The Rest is Politics, claimed by 2024 to be reaching 650,000 listeners per episode. When Campbell and former Conservative cabinet minister Rory Stewart take it on tour they fill stadiums. (“People like the podcast,” Campbell quipped at the press club.) Together, they have tapped into a large market of people who share their broadly centrist, cosmopolitan sensibilities.

Campbell’s appearance in Australia is partly another classic case of “man writes book.” The new title is Persevilience, his term for the blend of perseverance and resilience that he hopes will galvanise sensible citizens the world over to turn challenging situations into a better, brighter future. This lexical innovation hints at a broadly empowering, motivational, self-help type of message, laced with a streak of optimism.

Campbell’s ambition is to combat the three largest obstacles to a healthier politics: a “populism” that exploits rather than solves real problems; “polarisation” that purveys “fear and loathing for those with differing views”; and “post-truth,” specifically the “industrial-scale distortion and lying” that often passes for political rhetoric. Persevilience is what the world needs, he argues, in the face of political and media despots who masquerade as tribunes but rule as tyrants.

A cynic might dismiss all this as a celebrity’s attempt to sell books and stay relevant, but Campbell obviously cares deeply about the health of modern democracies, especially his own. His critiques of the media are particularly compelling. He argues that its pursuit of “balance” has come at the expense of accuracy, and that partisan, commercial self-interest on the part of moguls and journalists has undermined public institutions and integrity. He uses the Trump presidency and the rise of right-wing zealots from Nigel Farage to Pauline Hanson as examples, though it is the United Kingdom’s decision to leave the European Union that still stings him most.

Rupert Murdoch, that consequential Australian expatriate whose outlets helped shape the environment that birthed “Brexit,” looms large in Campbell’s analysis of modern media’s shortcomings. He reminds us that he was among the victims of Murdoch’s News of the World phone-hacking exploits. Though he initially hoped social media would “help break down the old media oligarchies” like Murdoch’s, Campbell now sees those platforms as uniquely harmful for good political discourse and especially for young people.

They have also been particularly dangerous for the elected representatives whose work makes them an emotional and sometimes physical target for disaffected members of the public. Herein lay the other chief occasion for Campbell’s address: the launching of the Better Politics Foundation’s Fit to Lead report on the “experiences, wellbeing and safety of being a politician in Australia.” Its findings show that 71 per cent of state and federal parliamentarians find their wellbeing “adversely impacted” by their job, and that social media is their “top stressor.”

A mental health activist who has been transparent and earnest in recounting his struggles with depression, Campbell was anxious to promote a fairer, more civil and less inhospitable political environment. Appealing to Australia’s strong democratic traditions, he suggested this country could “take a lead” in showing the world what a strong body politic and healthy media ecosystem can look like. It would require the media to hold politicians accountable without engaging in harmful demonisation, and individual citizens to practise and demand a healthier style of political discourse. These are noble injunctions, though it was hard not to notice his references to his populist opponents as “crooks” and “chancers.”

Campbell’s notion of persevilience is intended to promote a feeling of empowerment and political agency, for the modern global citizenry but especially for its youth. Young people are “not wrong,” he argued, to bemoan the “robotic” qualities of public discourse and the poor quality of modern journalism. Prompted during questions, Campbell declared that young people still have the power to overturn the political and economic settings that alienate them from civic life, the housing market, employment in AI-exposed industries and plenty else besides. But it was hard to escape the feeling Campbell was doing some projecting, seeing in young people’s anxieties for civic life a vivid reflection of his own concerns.

Commercial media occupies a very large place in the Campbell story. Both he and his partner Fiona Millar are industry veterans, and as a Daily Mirror journalist the young Alastair saw how newspapers could easily become pro-Tory partisans. Alluding to his strained relations with the British press while serving in Downing Street, he said he was often called a “liar, bully and worse” for his efforts to prosecute the government’s arguments. (“I deny the charges, milord,” he remarked to general mirth.)

Campbell is discerning in his criticisms of contemporary legacy media. Gesturing to the journalists who stand up to political despots or report from dangerous conflict zones, he laments that “too much of the world is off-limits to journalism.” He also celebrates those journalists who keep showing up to Donald Trump’s White House press briefings and asking the hard questions knowing that abuse awaits them.

Journalists, he says, should more often rise above their competitive imperatives and partisan instincts in order to defend their shared civic obligations. “If I had ever lied or bullied as much as Trump does,” he said on Monday, “I would have expected the entire Westminster press to walk out.” Alluding to former Trump staffer Kellyanne Conway and evoking the memory of venerated British journalist C.P. Scott, Campbell remarked, “I think Scott would have struggled with the concept of ‘alternative facts’, as should we all, because it is anathema to good journalism and to democracy.”

Scott, it is worth recalling, was a politician as well as a newspaperman. In fact, around the turn of the twentieth century he was both at the same time. Media historian Mark Hampton has shown that Scott believed in an “educationalist” role for the Manchester Guardian (of which he was longstanding editor) but also dictated its editorial line on issues as significant as the Boer War, which he also vocally opposed on the hustings and in the House of Commons.

Campbell recognises there have “always been” media moguls and pressmen who felt themselves “entitled to influence” over politics. But this power was tempered, he says, by a shared respect for facts and a broad acceptance of the fourth estate’s “democratic functions.” Now, “perhaps for the first time,” the likes of Trump and X owner Elon Musk see the public interest “purely as an extension of their own.”

But is it wise to treat Trump, Musk and their peers as historically anomalous, rather than as products of the same privately owned sector in which Campbell cut his teeth? Yes, business models and technologies have changed, but the media’s influence was always great. In his exceptional book What is Free Speech? historian Fara Dabhoiwala reminds us that earlier generations of media critics took for granted that “the incentives of private media companies are never aligned with the public good, however we might define that.” Campbell’s screeds against Murdoch are of a piece with that tradition.

A return to the time before Trump, Musk and Fox News may seem an inviting prospect for those who ruled the political and media roost thirty years ago. But the impulse sits awkwardly alongside an argument for a more civil, less partisan style of journalism motivated first and foremost by the public interest. It takes a real romantic to look at the 1980s or 1990s and see those ideals in common practice.

As it happens, Campbell is right to say that younger voters want more trustworthy news. Data from the 2026 Digital News Report, produced by the University of Canberra’s News and Media Research Centre, shows that left-leaning and right-leaning voters share similar levels of anxiety about misinformation online. Fears of a future where news is even more relentlessly partisan and overpopulated with AI-generated slop are not unfounded.

New mechanisms and initiatives are needed to safeguard public trust in news and information for the years ahead. The federal government’s Digital Duty of Care laws, inclusive of greater personal agency over social media algorithms and an individual right to sue big tech providers, are a timely step in that direction. A Finnish-style media literacy education for very young kids could also be worth considering, as Campbell suggests. The lofty Enlightenment ideal that the truth would always prevail in a properly functioning public sphere was barely tenable in its heyday; it is certainly untenable now.

Campbell was in reliably good form. He bowled up excellent lines and batted away with ease the questions he wished to avoid — questions about the unpopularity of prime minister Anthony Albanese, for instance. He is a man who always knows what performance a particular moment demands, whether it be warm sincerity for a discussion about mental health fiery invective in a clash with pro-Brexit apologists. At the press club, Campbell had most of the journalists and politicos spellbound.

His former boss, Tony Blair, was also exceptionally gifted at striking the right poses. Campbell described Blair on Monday as a skilled long-term strategist and “better communicator” than the recently deposed Keir Starmer. Yet their emphasis on style and performance was also what made the whole political project of “New Labour, New Britain” seem so shallow and ephemeral to its critics. In his interviews with Derek Reilly, the late Bob Hawke — no slouch in the performativity department — once dismissed Blair as “an actor.”

Hawke’s critique was hardly unique. In a recent documentary on The Tony Blair Story, broadcaster Andrew Neil remarked that New Labour had an “obsession with spin.” It is easy to dismiss such musings as partisan critiques from heroes of hindsight, but these sentiments were circulating at the time. The opening of London’s feted Millennium Dome in December 1999 was widely panned as the outward expression of New Labour’s “preference for style over content.” This was well before Blair led the UK into its disastrous adventure in Iraq.

And there stands arguably the biggest elephant in the room. At the press club, “Iraq” was mentioned just once, and by the host rather than the visitor. Campbell’s speech took truth and lying as its core themes, so the omission was not insignificant. That military deployment was the most controversial action of Blair’s decade in power, and one that placed Campbell in direct conflict with the media. A BBC journalist accused him of “sexing up” the British government’s fifty-page dossier on Iraq’s alleged weapons of mass destruction, released in September 2002 in a manner resembling “the launch of a bestseller.”

Today, Campbell is a keen proponent of the BBC and its bravery in the face of Trump’s self-indulgent libel suit over its portrayal of the 6 January insurrection. He sees the public broadcaster as a potential source of “soft power” in a world hungry for reliable information. In 2003, though, he was unflinching in his condemnation of the BBC’s “fundamental attack on the integrity of the government” and its “lie” about his and Blair’s handling of the infamous dossier. The landmark Chilcot inquiry into the war found “no evidence” of either man’s improper interference in its contents, but Campbell by his own admission provided “presentational” support for its publication.

As well as being a tactical mistake, the dossier seems likely to have been injurious to long-term political trust. As British security expert Robert Dover puts it, the whole affair taught a segment of the British public that “experts were often wrong” and that “politicians could not be trusted.” Though the evidence is scanter in the Australian context, Iraq was similarly divisive here. Not for nothing did then-senator Bob Brown call his private senator’s bill for an Iraq inquiry the “Invasion of Iraq Royal Commission (Restoring Public Trust in Government) Bill 2004.”

Of course, advisers advise and ministers decide. Blair carries the British public’s opprobrium for Iraq. Campbell served his prime minister with distinction. But his argument for truth and integrity — for a politics conducted in good faith — requires us to forget Iraq entirely and move on. If sandpapergate holds any lessons at all, it is surely that forgetting and moving on doesn’t always work. Campbell’s cheeky, abrasive prop notwithstanding, a critic with a long memory would be within their rights to find the whole performance a little too smooth for comfort. •
